title: Saltimbocca alla Romana
subtitle: Veal escalopes with sage and prosciutto in white wine
excerpt: Thin veal escalopes layered with a sage leaf and a slice of prosciutto, pan-fried quickly, then finished with white wine and butter. A Roman classic that cooks in under 10 minutes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Saltimbocca means jump in the mouth in Italian, a reference to how quickly it should be eaten after cooking. The dish is firmly associated with Roman trattoria cooking, though versions exist across central Italy. The pairing of veal, sage, and prosciutto is a Roman classic, and the dish should be cooked fast at high heat so the prosciutto crisps and the veal stays tender.

content.text: The key to saltimbocca is heat and speed. The pan must be hot when the escalopes go in, and the whole dish is done in minutes. Secure the prosciutto and sage to the veal with a cocktail stick so it doesn't lift off during cooking. The escalopes should be very thin, if your butcher has not already beaten them, do so between two sheets of cling film with a rolling pin.
Lay each escalope flat. Place 2 sage leaves on top, then a slice of prosciutto. Press down and secure with a cocktail stick. Dust very lightly in flour on the veal side only.

Heat half the butter and the olive oil in a large frying pan over high heat. When foaming, add the escalopes prosciutto-side down. Cook for 2 minutes until the prosciutto crisps. Flip and cook the veal side for 1 minute. Remove to a plate, do not stack.

Pour off excess fat. Add the wine to the hot pan and let it bubble and reduce for 2 minutes, scraping the pan. Add the remaining butter and swirl until emulsified into a glossy sauce. Season with salt and pepper.
Remove the cocktail sticks. Plate the saltimbocca with the sauce spooned over and serve immediately with sautéed courgette or a simple salad.
